statement: Let $(\mathfrak A,\bar\mu)$ be a [measure algebra](c:measure-algebra) with $\bar\mu 1 = 1$. Then $\mathfrak A$ is a product of countably many [atoms](c:atom) and, for countably many infinite cardinals $\kappa$, one scaled copy of the measure algebra of $\{0,1\}^\kappa$. The atom masses and the masses at each $\kappa$ determine $\mathfrak A$ up to isomorphism.

hypotheses.text: The pair $(\mathfrak A,\bar\mu)$ is a [measure algebra](c:measure-algebra): a $\sigma$-complete [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) with a strictly positive countably additive measure.
The total mass is finite, so after scaling $\bar\mu 1 = 1$.

conclusion: The algebra $\mathfrak A$ is isomorphic to the product of its atoms and of one scaled algebra $\{0,1\}^\kappa$ for each weight $\kappa$ in a countable set, and the atom masses and the masses at each $\kappa$ are a complete isomorphism invariant.

proofs.name: Decomposition into homogeneous pieces
proofs.slogan: Split off the atoms, cut the rest into homogeneous pieces, and identify each piece with a cube algebra by an independent family.
proofs.scope: The probability case; a finite measure is rescaled to total mass $1$. The independent-family step and the uniqueness are long, so this outline names what the cited text does at each step.

roles.why: The $\sigma$-complete [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) and the positive measure make principal ideals, atoms and Maharam types behave.
Finite mass makes the atoms countable and gives every independent element mass one half after scaling.

steps.slogan: Split off the [atoms](c:atom), which are countably many.
steps.detail: The atoms have positive masses with sum at most $1$, so there are countably many. Their supremum $a$ gives a purely atomic factor, and the principal ideal of the complement of $a$ has no atoms.

steps.slogan: Cut the atomless part into homogeneous pieces by Maharam type.
steps.detail: The Maharam type of an algebra is the least size of a generating set. A Zorn argument gives a partition of unity whose principal ideals have one type at every nonzero part, and pieces of equal type merge into one piece for each infinite cardinal $\kappa$ (Fremlin, section 332).

steps.slogan: Find an [independent family](c:independent-family-of-sets) of size $\kappa$ in each homogeneous piece.
steps.detail: By transfinite induction on $\kappa$: an algebra generated by fewer than $\kappa$ elements has smaller type, so homogeneity gives, under every nonzero part, a new element of mass one half independent of the earlier ones. The $\kappa$ elements generate the piece (Fremlin, section 331).

steps.slogan: Match the independent family with the [product measure](c:product-measure) on $\{0,1\}^\kappa$.
steps.detail: Independent elements of mass one half have the joint distribution of the coordinate sets of $\{0,1\}^\kappa$, so the coordinate map preserves the measure of the generated algebra. It extends to a measure-preserving isomorphism of the completions (Fremlin, theorem 331I).

steps.slogan: Show that the weights and masses are isomorphism invariants and read off the classification.
steps.detail: The Maharam type of principal ideals does not change under a measure-preserving isomorphism, so the atom masses and the masses of the pieces of each weight $\kappa$ are determined by $\mathfrak A$. Algebras with equal data are isomorphic piece by piece.

concepts.c:measure-algebra: The theorem classifies these algebras up to measure-preserving isomorphism.
concepts.c:boolean-algebra: Suprema and principal ideals of the algebra drive every step.
concepts.c:atom: Atoms are the minimal nonzero elements and form the purely atomic factor.
concepts.c:independent-family-of-sets: Independent half-mass elements play the role of the cube coordinates.
concepts.c:product-measure: The cube carries the product measure that the independent family reproduces.

source.ref: D. H. Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volume 3: Measure Algebras, Torres Fremlin, Colchester, 2002, sections 331 and 332, after D. Maharam, On homogeneous measure algebras, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 28 (1942), 108-111.
source.note: Fremlin proves the homogeneous case in section 331 (theorem 331I) and the general classification in section 332; the steps follow that order.

statement: Let $\alpha$ be a finite [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) with $\top \ne \bot$ and let $s \subseteq \alpha$ be an [intersecting family](c:intersecting-family): $a \wedge b \ne \bot$ for all $a, b \in s$. Then $2|s| \le |\alpha|$, and $s$ is maximal among intersecting families exactly when $2|s| = |\alpha|$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $\alpha$ is a finite [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) with $\top \ne \bot$.
The family $s$ is [intersecting](c:intersecting-family): $a \wedge b \ne \bot$ for all $a, b \in s$.

conclusion: The family has at most $|\alpha|/2$ members, and it is maximal if and only if it has exactly $|\alpha|/2$ members.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the equivalence between maximality and $2|s| = |\alpha|$. The bound $2|s| \le |\alpha|$ is the separate declaration Set.Intersecting.card_le, which the proof uses.

proofs.name: Complement pairs
proofs.slogan: Pair each element with its complement, then count: a maximal family is an up-set that holds one of each pair.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for every finite nontrivial Boolean algebra. The empty family is intersecting and is handled by the case $a = \bot$ in the step on maximal families.

roles.why: Finiteness lets the proof count, and every element has a [complement](c:is-compl); $\top \ne \bot$ makes $\{\top\}$ an intersecting family.
The meets $a \wedge b \ne \bot$ show that $a$ and its complement are not both in $s$ and justify every insertion.

steps.slogan: Pair each member with its [complement](c:is-compl) to bound the size.
steps.detail: For $a \in s$ we have $a \wedge a^c = \bot$, so $a^c \notin s$. Hence $s$ and $\{a^c : a \in s\}$ are disjoint subsets of $\alpha$ of equal size, and $2|s| \le |\alpha|$.

steps.slogan: Show that a family with $2|s| = |\alpha|$ is maximal.
steps.detail: Let $t \supseteq s$ be intersecting. By the bound, $2|t| \le |\alpha| = 2|s| \le 2|t|$, so $|t| = |s|$, and $s = t$ because $s \subseteq t$ are finite sets of equal size.

steps.slogan: Show that a maximal intersecting family is an up-set.
steps.detail: Let $a \in s$ and $a \le b$. Then $b \ne \bot$, and $c \wedge a \le c \wedge b$ gives $c \wedge b \ne \bot$ for every $c \in s$. So $s \cup \{b\}$ is intersecting, and maximality gives $b \in s$.

steps.slogan: Show that a maximal family holds $a$ or $a^c$ for every $a$.
steps.detail:
Suppose $a

steps.slogan: Count the maximal family to get $2|s| = |\alpha|$.
steps.detail: The sets $s$ and $\{a^c : a \in s\}$ are disjoint, and by the previous step they cover $\alpha$. So $|\alpha| = |s| + |s|$.

steps.detail: Step one gives $2|s| \le |\alpha|$. Step two gives that $2|s| = |\alpha|$ implies maximal, and step five gives the converse.

concepts.c:boolean-algebra: Complements and finiteness make the pairing and the count possible.
concepts.c:intersecting-family: The family is the object whose size and maximality are studied.
concepts.c:is-compl: An element and its complement have meet $\bot$, so they are never both in $s$.

source.note: mathlib uses the bound Set.Intersecting.card_le (complement pairs, Intersecting.disjoint_map_compl), shows that a maximal family is an up-set (Intersecting.isUpperSet') and that it holds a or its complement.

statement: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $X$ be a grouplike algebra over the little $n$-cubes [operad](c:e-n-operad), that is, $\pi_0 X$ is a group. Then $X$ is weakly equivalent, as an $E_n$-algebra, to the $n$-fold [loop space](c:loop-space) $\Omega^n B^n X$. Conversely, every $n$-fold loop space is such an algebra.

hypotheses.text: The integer $n$ satisfies $n \ge 1$.
The space $X$ is an algebra over the little $n$-cubes [operad](c:e-n-operad) $E_n$.
The monoid $\pi_0 X$ is a group.

conclusion: The space $X$ is weakly equivalent to $\Omega^n B^n X$ as an $E_n$-algebra, so it is an $n$-fold loop space, and every $\Omega^n Y$ is a grouplike $E_n$-algebra.

proofs.name: Bar construction and approximation theorem
proofs.slogan: Build the delooping by an iterated bar construction and compare it with the free case by the approximation theorem.
proofs.scope: Well-pointed compactly generated spaces, as in the source. The approximation theorem and the comparison of bar constructions rest on May's book, so this is an outline.

roles.why: The $n$ loop coordinates need $n \ge 1$, and the delooping uses $n$ suspensions.
The action of the little cubes [operad](c:e-n-operad) gives the monad $C_n$ that the bar construction uses.
A group $\pi_0 X$ lets the bar construction commute with $n$-fold loops, and the approximation theorem becomes a [group completion](c:group-completion) there.

steps.slogan: Give each [loop space](c:loop-space) the structure of a little cubes algebra.
steps.detail: Insert $k$ loops into $k$ disjoint little cubes of $I^n$ and send the rest of the cube to the base point. This makes $\Omega^n Y$ an $E_n$-algebra with $\pi_0 = \pi_n Y$ a group, which is the easy direction.

steps.slogan: Build $B^n X$ by an iterated [bar construction](c:bar-construction).
steps.detail: May forms the two-sided bar construction $B(\Sigma^n, C_n, X)$ from the monad $C_n$ of the operad. It gives the space $B^n X$ and a natural map $X \to \Omega^n B^n X$.

steps.slogan: Prove the approximation theorem for free algebras.
steps.detail: For connected $Z$, the map $C_n Z \to \Omega^n \Sigma^n Z$ is a weak equivalence, and in general it is a [group completion](c:group-completion). May proves this with configuration spaces labelled by $Z$.

steps.slogan: Resolve $X$ by free algebras and compare the two bar constructions.
steps.detail: The bar construction $B(C_n, C_n, X)$ is equivalent to $X$. For grouplike $X$ the map to $B(\Omega^n \Sigma^n, C_n, X)$ is an equivalence by the approximation theorem, and this space is equivalent to $\Omega^n B(\Sigma^n, C_n, X)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $X \simeq \Omega^n B^n X$ and combine with the easy direction.
steps.detail: Steps three and four give the weak equivalence $X \to \Omega^n B^n X$ of $E_n$-algebras, so $X$ is an $n$-fold loop space. Step one gives the converse.

concepts.c:e-n-operad: Its algebras are the spaces with $n$ compatible multiplications.
concepts.c:loop-space: Iterated loop spaces are the model that the recognition principle identifies.
concepts.c:bar-construction: The bar construction delooping $X$ is the heart of the comparison.
concepts.c:group-completion: The approximation theorem is a group completion for non-connected $Z$.

source.ref: J. P. May, The Geometry of Iterated Loop Spaces, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 271, Springer, Berlin, 1972.
source.note: May proves the approximation theorem and the recognition principle for the little cubes operads $C_n$ with the bar construction $B(\Sigma^n, C_n, X)$.

statement: Let $G \subseteq \mathbb C$ be a [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) domain and $f$ an analytic function element at $a \in G$ that has an [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) along every path in $G$ from $a$. Then the continuation to $z$ does not depend on the path, and these continuations form one analytic function $F$ on $G$ with $F = f$ near $a$.

hypotheses.text: The set $G$ is a [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) domain in $\mathbb C$.
The function element $f$ at $a \in G$ is an [analytic function](c:analytic-function) on a disc around $a$.
The element $f$ has an [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) along every path in $G$ that starts at $a$.

conclusion: There is an analytic function $F$ on $G$ with $F = f$ near $a$, and near each $z \in G$ the function $F$ is the continuation of $f$ along every path from $a$ to $z$.

proofs.name: Homotopy and chains of discs
proofs.slogan: Show that continuation along a path does not change under a homotopy with fixed ends, then use simple connectivity.
proofs.scope: Paths are continuous maps $[0,1] \to G$ and homotopies fix both end points. The case of a constant path shows that $F = f$ near $a$.

roles.why: Simple connectivity makes any two paths from $a$ to $z$ [homotopic](c:homotopy) with fixed ends.
The element $f$ is the starting germ of every continuation.
Continuation exists along every path of a homotopy, so the end elements are defined for all of them.

steps.slogan: Describe a continuation along a path by a chain of discs.
steps.detail: A continuation along $\gamma$ is a family of elements $(f_t, D_t)$ with $f_s = f_t$ near $\gamma(t)$ for $s$ close to $t$. By compactness of $[0,1]$ there are $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_m = 1$ and discs $D_j \supseteq \gamma([t_{j-1}, t_j])$ with elements $f_j$ that agree on consecutive overlaps.

steps.slogan: Show that the continuation along a path is unique.
steps.detail: Two continuations of $f$ along $\gamma$ agree at each step: two analytic functions on a connected disc that agree on a nonempty open set agree on the disc. So the end element along $\gamma$ is determined by $f$ and $\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Show that nearby paths of a homotopy have the same end element.
steps.detail: Let $H$ be a homotopy of paths $\gamma_s$ from $a$ to $b$ and fix $s_0$ with a chain for $\gamma_{s_0}$. By uniform continuity of $H$, for $s$ near $s_0$ each $\gamma_s([t_{j-1}, t_j])$ lies in $D_j$, so the same chain continues $f$ along $\gamma_s$. By uniqueness the end elements at $b$ agree.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the end element is constant along the whole homotopy.
steps.detail: By the previous step the end element at $b$ of $\gamma_s$ is locally constant in $s$. The interval $[0,1]$ is connected, so $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ give the same end element.

steps.slogan: Define $F$ with simple connectivity and check that it is analytic.
steps.detail: Two paths from $a$ to $z$ in the [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) set $G$ are homotopic with fixed ends, so they give the same element at $z$. Let $F(z)$ be the value of this element at $z$. Near $z$ the function $F$ equals an [analytic](c:analytic-function) element, and the constant path shows $F = f$ near $a$.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: It supplies a homotopy between any two paths with the same ends.
concepts.c:analytic-continuation: The proof studies how continuation along a path depends on the path.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Analytic elements on discs are the objects continued along paths.
concepts.c:homotopy: Homotopies with fixed ends are the families along which the end element stays constant.

source.note: The classical chain-of-discs proof, as in Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapter 16 (the monodromy theorem).

statement: Let $A$, $K$ and $H$ be [finite sets](c:finite-set). There is a finite set $\iota$ such that every colouring $C \colon A^\iota \to K$ is constant on some [combinatorial subspace](c:combinatorial-subspace) of dimension $|H|$ in $A^\iota$.

hypotheses.text: The alphabet $A$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set).
The set $K$ of colours is finite.
The index set $H$ of the dimension is finite.

conclusion: Some [combinatorial subspace](c:combinatorial-subspace) of $A^\iota$ with $|H|$ variable blocks is monochromatic for $C$.

formal.difference: The statements agree in substance. Mathlib indexes the dimension by a finite type $\eta$ and encodes a subspace as a map $\iota \to \alpha \oplus \eta$ that uses every element of $\eta$.

proofs.name: Lines over a large alphabet
proofs.slogan: Apply the Hales-Jewett theorem to the alphabet of all functions from $H$ to $A$ and read each line as a subspace.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for any finite alphabet, colour set and dimension. The case $H = \emptyset$ is trivial, and the proof covers it with the same construction.

roles.why: A finite alphabet makes $A^H$ finite, and the Hales-Jewett theorem needs a finite alphabet.
A finite colour set is required by the Hales-Jewett theorem.
A finite $H$ keeps $A^H$ finite and gives the $|H|$ variable blocks.

steps.slogan: Form the large alphabet $B = A^H$ of all functions from $H$ to $A$.
steps.detail: Since $A$ and $H$ are [finite](c:finite-set), $B$ is finite. We treat $B$ as a new alphabet and look at $B^N$ for an index set $N$ chosen next.

steps.slogan: Apply the Hales-Jewett theorem to the alphabet $B$ and the colour set $K$.
steps.detail: The theorem gives a finite set $N$ such that every colouring $B^N \to K$ has a monochromatic combinatorial line.

steps.slogan: Identify $B^N$ with $A^{N \times H}$ and move the colouring across.
steps.detail: A point of $B^N$ is a family $(x_i)_{i \in N}$ with $x_i \colon H \to A$, which is the function $(i,h) \mapsto x_i(h)$ on $N \times H$. Put $\iota = N \times H$; a colouring of $A^\iota$ becomes a colouring of $B^N$.

steps.slogan: Turn the monochromatic line into a map $A^H \to A^\iota$ with $|H|$ variable blocks.
steps.detail: The line has a nonempty set $S \subseteq N$ of moving coordinates and fixed values $b_i \in B$ for $i \notin S$. For $x \in A^H$ put coordinate $(i,h)$ equal to $x(h)$ if $i \in S$ and to $b_i(h)$ otherwise. The variable $h$ then fills the nonempty block $S \times \{h\}$, so the image is a [combinatorial subspace](c:combinatorial-subspace) of dimension $|H|$.

steps.slogan: Check that the subspace is monochromatic.
steps.detail: The image of $x \in A^H = B$ is the point of the line at parameter $x$. The line is monochromatic, so $C$ takes one value on the whole subspace.

concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness of the alphabet and of $H$ keeps the large alphabet finite.
concepts.c:combinatorial-subspace: The monochromatic line becomes the required subspace of dimension $|H|$.

source.note: mathlib applies Combinatorics.Line.exists_mono_in_high_dimension to the alphabet $\eta \to \alpha$ and reindexes the line by $\iota \times \eta$ (Line.toSubspace and Subspace.reindex).

statement: Let $X$ be a [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space) [regular space](c:regular-space). Then $X$ is [metrizable](c:metrizable-space) if and only if $X$ has a [sigma-locally finite](c:sigma-locally-finite) base, that is, a base that is a countable union of [locally finite families](c:locally-finite-family).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space).
The space $X$ is [regular](c:regular-space): a point and a closed set that misses it have disjoint open neighborhoods.

conclusion: The space $X$ is metrizable exactly when it has a sigma-locally finite base.

proofs.name: Locally finite refinements and an embedding
proofs.slogan: Get the base from locally finite refinements of ball covers, and get the metric from an embedding built from Urysohn functions.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The direction from a metric uses no hypothesis, because metric spaces are Hausdorff and regular.

roles.why: Points are closed, so two different points are separated by a basis set, and the embedding is injective.
Regularity shrinks each basis set to a basis set with closed neighborhood inside it, which gives the $F_\sigma$ and normality steps.

steps.slogan: Build a base from locally finite refinements of the ball covers.
steps.detail: Let $d$ be a metric. A metric space is [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) by Stone's theorem, so the cover by balls of radius $1/m$ has a locally finite open refinement $\mathcal B_m$. If $B(x, 2/m) \subseteq U$ with $U$ open, some $V \in \mathcal B_m$ has $x \in V \subseteq B(x,2/m) \subseteq U$, so $\bigcup_m \mathcal B_m$ is a sigma-locally finite [base](c:base).

steps.slogan: Show that every open set is a countable union of closed sets.
steps.detail: For $U$ open, regularity puts each $x \in U$ in some $W \in \mathcal B = \bigcup_n \mathcal B_n$ with $\overline W \subseteq U$. Let $C_n$ be the union of the $W \in \mathcal B_n$ with $\overline W \subseteq U$; a locally finite union of closed sets is closed, so $\overline{C_n} = \bigcup \overline W \subseteq U$ and $U = \bigcup_n \overline{C_n}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $X$ is [normal](c:normal-space).
steps.detail: Let $E, F$ be disjoint closed sets. By regularity $E \subseteq \bigcup_n C_n$, where $C_n$ unites the $W \in \mathcal B_n$ with $\overline W \cap F = \emptyset$, and $\overline{C_n} \cap F = \emptyset$ by local finiteness; define $D_n$ for $F$ in the same way. The open sets $\bigcup_n (C_n \setminus \bigcup_{i \le n} \overline{D_i})$ and $\bigcup_n (D_n \setminus \bigcup_{i \le n} \overline{C_i})$ contain $E$ and $F$ and are disjoint.

steps.slogan: Build a continuous function that is positive exactly on each basis set.
steps.detail: For $W \in \mathcal B_n$ the set $X \setminus W$ is closed and, by the previous steps, equals $\bigcap_k U_k$ with $U_k$ open. Urysohn's lemma gives continuous $g_k \colon X \to [0,1]$ with $g_k = 0$ on $X \setminus W$ and $g_k = 1$ off $U_k$. Then $f_W = \frac1n \sum_k 2^{-k} g_k$ is continuous, has values in $[0, 1/n]$, and is positive exactly on $W$.

steps.slogan: Define $F(x) = (f_W(x))_W$ and show that it is continuous.
steps.detail: Index the functions by $J = \{(n,W) : W \in \mathcal B_n\}$ and give $[0,1]^J$ the metric $\rho(z,w) = \sup_J |z_j - w_j|$. Fix $x_0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ and take $N > 2/\varepsilon$, so values with $n > N$ are at most $1/N$. For $n \le N$ some neighborhood of $x_0$ meets finitely many $W \in \mathcal B_n$; shrinking it keeps those values within $\varepsilon/2$, and the others stay $0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $X$ is homeomorphic to a metric space.

concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Hausdorff separation makes the embedding map injective.
concepts.c:regular-space: Regularity gives the closed neighborhoods inside basis sets that the proof needs.
concepts.c:metrizable-space: The embedding into a metric space is what makes $X$ metrizable.
concepts.c:sigma-locally-finite: A countable union of locally finite families controls each coordinate of the embedding.
concepts.c:locally-finite-family: Local finiteness makes unions of closures closed and each coordinate sum finite.
concepts.c:paracompact-space: Paracompactness of metric spaces gives the locally finite refinements.
concepts.c:base: The refinements together form the base that the theorem requires.
concepts.c:normal-space: Normality gives Urysohn functions for the basis sets.

source.note: The standard proof, as in Munkres, Topology, 2nd edition, section 40 (the Nagata-Smirnov theorem), with Stone's theorem that metrizable spaces are paracompact.

statement: Let $E \colon y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ be an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) with $a, b \in \mathbb Z$ and $D = 4a^3 + 27b^2 \ne 0$, and let $P = (x, y) \ne O$ be a rational [torsion point](c:torsion-point) of $E$. Then $x, y \in \mathbb Z$, and either $y = 0$ or $y^2$ divides $D$, the [discriminant](c:discriminant) up to sign.

hypotheses.text: The curve $E \colon y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ has integers $a, b$ and $D = 4a^3 + 27b^2 \ne 0$, so $E$ is an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve).
The point $P = (x, y) \ne O$ is rational and has finite order, so it is a [torsion point](c:torsion-point).

conclusion: The coordinates $x$ and $y$ are integers, and either $y = 0$ or $y^2 \mid D$.

proofs.name: Formal group and duplication
proofs.slogan: Show integrality prime by prime with the formal group, then divide using the duplication formula and a polynomial identity.
proofs.scope: Short Weierstrass form over $\mathbb Q$ with integral coefficients. The integrality steps rest on the formal group results of the cited book; the divisibility step is proved here.

roles.why: Integral coefficients make non-integral points land in the formal-group subgroup, and make the final identity an identity in $\mathbb Z[x]$.
Finite order bounds the valuation of $x$ at each prime, and $2P$ is again a torsion point.

steps.slogan: Place a non-integral point in the formal-group subgroup at a prime.
steps.detail: Suppose $x$ or $y$ is not an integer. Since $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ has integral coefficients, some prime $p$ has $v_p(x) = -2r$ and $v_p(y) = -3r$ with $r \ge 1$. These are the points of the subgroup $E_1(\mathbb Q_p)$, which the [formal group](c:formal-group) of $E$ parametrizes.

steps.slogan: Bound the valuation of a torsion point at a prime.
steps.detail: By Silverman, theorem VII.3.4, a torsion point of exact order $m \ge 2$ is $p$-integral unless $m = p^k$, and then $v_p(x) \ge -2/(p^k - p^{k-1})$. If $p^k - p^{k-1} \ge 2$ this gives $v_p(x) \ge -1$, against $v_p(x) = -2r \le -2$.

steps.slogan: Treat the one exceptional case, a point of order two at the prime two.
steps.detail: The bound leaves only $p = 2$ and $k = 1$, so $P$ has order $2$. Then $y = 0$ and $x$ is a rational root of the monic integer cubic $x^3 + ax + b$, so $x \in \mathbb Z$ by the rational root theorem, against $v_2(x) < 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $x$ and $y$ are integers.
steps.detail: No prime has $v_p(x) < 0$, so $x \in \mathbb Z$. Then $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b \in \mathbb Z$ with $y$ rational gives $y \in \mathbb Z$.

steps.slogan: Double the point and use that $2P$ is again an integral torsion point.
steps.detail: If $y \ne 0$, then $2P \ne O$ is a torsion point, so $x(2P) \in \mathbb Z$ by the first part. The duplication formula gives $x(2P) = g(x)/(4y^2)$ with $g(x) = x^4 - 2ax^2 - 8bx + a^2$, so $4y^2 \mid g(x)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the divisibility with a polynomial identity to get $y^2 \mid D$.
steps.detail: With $f(x) = x^3 + ax + b$ one checks $(-3x^3 + 5ax + 27b)\, f(x) + (3x^2 + 4a)\, g(x) = 4a^3 + 27b^2$. Since $f(x) = y^2$ and $y^2 \mid g(x)$, the integer $y^2$ divides $D$.

concepts.c:elliptic-curve: The curve and its group law are the setting of the whole proof.
concepts.c:torsion-point: Finite order is what bounds the valuations and allows doubling.
concepts.c:discriminant: The number $D$ is the discriminant of the cubic up to sign.
concepts.c:formal-group: The formal group describes the points with negative valuation at a prime.

source.ref: J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd edition, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 106, Springer, New York, 2009, Chapter VII section 3 and Chapter VIII section 7.
source.note: Silverman derives integrality from the formal group (theorem VII.3.4) in section VIII.7; the divisibility step uses the duplication formula, as in Silverman and Tate, Rational Points on Elliptic Curves, chapter 2.

statement: Let $\rho$ and $\sigma$ be [density matrices](c:density-matrix) on a [finite-dimensional Hilbert space](c:finite-dimensional-hilbert-space) $\mathcal H$. A [quantum channel](c:quantum-channel) $\Lambda \colon \mathcal H \to \mathcal H \otimes \mathcal H$ with $\operatorname{tr}_2 \Lambda(\tau) = \operatorname{tr}_1 \Lambda(\tau) = \tau$ for $\tau \in \{\rho, \sigma\}$ exists if and only if $\rho\sigma = \sigma\rho$.

hypotheses.text: The space $\mathcal H$ is a [finite-dimensional Hilbert space](c:finite-dimensional-hilbert-space).
The operators $\rho$ and $\sigma$ are [density matrices](c:density-matrix) on $\mathcal H$.

conclusion: The states $\rho$ and $\sigma$ can be broadcast exactly when they commute, so noncommuting states cannot be broadcast.

proofs.name: Fidelity and purification
proofs.slogan: Copy in a common eigenbasis when the states commute; otherwise purify a broadcast and squeeze the fidelity at both marginals.
proofs.scope: Pairs of states on a finite-dimensional space. The step that turns the equal fidelities into commutation is the core of the cited paper and is not reproduced here.

roles.why: Finite dimension gives the common eigenbasis and the Stinespring dilation with matrices.
The two states are the inputs to broadcast and the purifications start from them.

steps.slogan: Copy in a common eigenbasis when the states commute.
steps.detail: Commuting Hermitian matrices have a common orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_i)$. The channel $\Lambda(\tau) = \sum_i \langle e_i|\tau|e_i\rangle\, |e_ie_i\rangle\langle e_ie_i|$ has both marginals equal to the diagonal part of $\tau$, which is $\tau$ itself for $\tau = \rho$ and $\tau = \sigma$.

steps.slogan: Dilate a broadcasting channel to an isometry.
steps.detail: A [completely positive](c:completely-positive-map) trace-preserving map $\Lambda$ has the form $\Lambda(\tau) = \operatorname{tr}_E V \tau V^\dagger$ for an isometry $V \colon \mathcal H \to \mathcal H_A \otimes \mathcal H_B \otimes \mathcal H_E$ (Stinespring). Suppose that $\Lambda$ broadcasts $\rho$ and $\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Take optimal purifications and push them through the isometry.
steps.detail: Uhlmann's theorem gives [pure states](c:pure-state) $\psi$ and $\varphi$ on $\mathcal H \otimes \mathcal R$ that purify $\rho$ and $\sigma$ with $\langle\psi|\varphi\rangle = F(\rho,\sigma)$. The isometry $V \otimes 1$ keeps this overlap, so the images $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ have $\langle\Psi|\Phi\rangle = F(\rho,\sigma)$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze the fidelity of the broadcast states between two equal values.
steps.detail: $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ purify the broadcast states $\omega, \omega'$ on $AB$, whose marginals on $A$ and on $B$ are $\rho$ and $\sigma$. Monotonicity under the [partial trace](c:partial-trace-quantum-channel) gives $F(\rho,\sigma) = \langle\Psi|\Phi\rangle \le F(\omega,\omega') \le F(\rho,\sigma)$, so this overlap is optimal at $A$ and at $B$ together.

steps.slogan: Deduce commutation from the double optimality, as the cited paper does.
steps.detail: The cited paper shows that two pure states that are optimal purifications for both marginals force $\rho\sigma = \sigma\rho$. This deduction is not reproduced here.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: If $\rho$ and $\sigma$ commute, step one broadcasts them. If a channel broadcasts them, steps two to five give $\rho\sigma = \sigma\rho$.

concepts.c:finite-dimensional-hilbert-space: Finite dimension makes eigenbases and Stinespring dilations concrete matrices.
concepts.c:density-matrix: The theorem concerns pairs of density matrices.
concepts.c:quantum-channel: A broadcast is a quantum channel with two prescribed marginals.
concepts.c:completely-positive-map: Complete positivity gives the Stinespring isometry of the channel.
concepts.c:pure-state: Purifications are pure states whose marginals are the given states.
concepts.c:partial-trace-quantum-channel: The marginals are partial traces, and fidelity cannot grow under them.

source.ref: H. Barnum, C. M. Caves, C. A. Fuchs, R. Jozsa and B. Schumacher, Noncommuting mixed states cannot be broadcast, Physical Review Letters 76 (1996), 2818-2821.
source.note: The paper copies in a common eigenbasis for commuting states and proves the converse with fidelity, purification and monotonicity under partial trace.

statement: Let $n \ge 1$ and give $\mathbb R^{2n}$ the standard form $\omega_0 = \sum_i dx_i \wedge dy_i$ of a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold). If the open ball $B^{2n}(r)$ embeds symplectically in the cylinder $Z^{2n}(R) = \{x_1^2 + y_1^2 < R^2\}$, then $r \le R$.

hypotheses.text: The dimension is $2n$ with $n \ge 1$.
There is a smooth embedding $\varphi \colon B^{2n}(r) \to Z^{2n}(R)$ with $\varphi^* \omega_0 = \omega_0$.

proofs.name: Pseudoholomorphic sphere through the center
proofs.slogan: Compactify the cylinder, find a pseudoholomorphic sphere through the center of the ball, and compare its area with the ball's.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 1$. The nonvanishing Gromov invariant and the compactness rest on Gromov's paper, so this is an outline; the area comparison is proved here.

roles.why: The $2n - 2$ extra directions of the cylinder are compactified by a torus.
The embedding carries the standard structure of the ball into the compact manifold, where the monotonicity inequality applies.

steps.slogan: Embed a slightly smaller closed ball in a closed symplectic manifold.
steps.detail: Fix $r' < r$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. The image of the closed ball $\overline B(r')$ is compact, so it lies in a bounded part of $Z(R)$, which embeds symplectically in $M = S^2(a) \times T^{2n-2}$. Here the sphere has area $a = \pi R^2 + \varepsilon$ and the torus is large and flat.

steps.slogan: Find a [pseudoholomorphic curve](c:pseudoholomorphic-curve) in the class $[S^2 \times \mathrm{pt}]$ through the center of the ball.
steps.detail: Choose an [almost complex structure](c:almost-complex-structure) $J$ on $M$, tamed by $\omega$ and standard on the image of the ball. For the product structure exactly one such sphere passes through a point, so the [Gromov invariant](c:gromov-witten-invariants) of the class is nonzero. Gromov compactness, with no bubbling because $a$ is the least sphere area, gives a $J$-sphere through the center for every tamed $J$.

steps.slogan: Bound from below the area of the curve inside the ball.
steps.detail: On the image of the ball $J$ is standard, so the part of the curve in the ball is a complex curve in $B^{2n}(r')$ through the center with boundary on the boundary sphere. Its area is at least $\pi r'^2$ by the monotonicity (Lelong) inequality.

steps.slogan: Compare the area of the sphere with the area inside the ball.
steps.detail: The sphere has area $\omega([S^2 \times \mathrm{pt}]) = a$, and every part of a $J$-curve has positive area because $J$ is tamed. So $\pi r'^2 \le a = \pi R^2 + \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon$ tend to zero and $r'$ tend to $r$.
steps.detail: The inequality $\pi r'^2 \le \pi R^2 + \varepsilon$ holds for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $r' < r$. Hence $r \le R$.

concepts.c:symplectic-manifold: The ball, the cylinder and the compact target are symplectic manifolds.
concepts.c:pseudoholomorphic-curve: A pseudoholomorphic sphere is the tool that measures the ball.
concepts.c:almost-complex-structure: The structure $J$ is chosen standard on the ball and tamed by $\omega$.
concepts.c:gromov-witten-invariants: A nonzero count of spheres guarantees one through the center for every $J$.

source.ref: M. Gromov, Pseudo holomorphic curves in symplectic manifolds, Inventiones Mathematicae 82 (1985), 307-347.
source.note: Gromov proves the theorem with $J$-holomorphic spheres in the product of a sphere and a torus.

statement: Let $T$ be Hilbert's [axioms](c:axiom) for the plane without the parallel axiom $P$: through a point off a line there is exactly one line missing it. The Euclidean plane is a [model](c:model) of $T + P$, and the Poincaré disc, a model of the [hyperbolic plane](c:hyperbolic-plane), satisfies $T + \neg P$. So neither $P$ nor $\neg P$ follows from $T$.

hypotheses.text: The theory $T$ consists of Hilbert's [axioms](c:axiom) of incidence, order, congruence and continuity for the plane.
The real numbers exist, so that $\mathbb R^2$ and the unit disc are available as structures.

conclusion: There is a [model](c:model) of $T$ in which $P$ holds and one in which $P$ fails, so neither $P$ nor $\neg P$ follows from $T$.

proofs.name: Euclidean and hyperbolic models
proofs.slogan: Check the axioms in two models, the Euclidean plane and the Poincaré disc, one where $P$ holds and one where it fails.
proofs.scope: Semantic independence: a consequence of $T$ holds in every model of $T$. The checks of the axioms in the disc are routine but long, so the steps name the key facts.

roles.why: The axioms of $T$ are what each model must satisfy, and what the disc check verifies.
The real numbers build the plane and the disc.

steps.slogan: Check that the Euclidean plane is a model of $T$ in which $P$ holds.
steps.detail: Take $\mathbb R^2$ with the usual lines, betweenness and Euclidean distance. The axioms of $T$ hold, continuity because $\mathbb R$ is complete and Archimedean. Through a point off a line there is exactly one [parallel](c:parallel-lines).

steps.slogan: Define the Poincaré disc: its points, lines and distance.
steps.detail: The points are the points of the open unit disc $D$. The lines are the diameters and the arcs of circles in $D$ orthogonal to the unit circle. The distance is $d(z,w) = \operatorname{arcosh}\bigl(1 + 2|z-w|^2/((1-|z|^2)(1-|w|^2))\bigr)$, and the Möbius maps of $D$ preserve lines and $d$.

steps.slogan: Check that the disc satisfies the axioms of $T$.
steps.detail: Two points lie on exactly one line: move one to $0$ by an [isometry](c:isometry) and use the diameter. Order along an arc and congruence by $d$ satisfy the axioms, because the isometries act transitively on flags, which gives side-angle-side. Each line is isometric to $\mathbb R$, which gives continuity.

steps.slogan: Show that $P$ fails in the disc.
steps.detail: Let $\ell$ be the horizontal diameter and $p = (0,t)$ with $0 < t < 1$. The line through $p$ orthogonal to the vertical diameter is an arc that stays above height $t$, so it misses $\ell$, and so do the lines through $p$ with a small turn from it. So infinitely many lines through $p$ miss $\ell$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $P$ is independent of $T$.
steps.detail: A consequence of $T$ holds in every model of $T$. The plane satisfies $P$, so $\neg P$ does not follow from $T$. The disc satisfies $T$ and not $P$, so $P$ does not follow from $T$.

concepts.c:axiom: The proof asks which statements follow from the other axioms.
concepts.c:model: A model that satisfies the axioms but not $P$ shows independence.
concepts.c:hyperbolic-plane: The Poincaré disc is the model of the hyperbolic plane.
concepts.c:parallel-lines: The failure of unique parallels is the property $P$ fails to have.
concepts.c:isometry: Isometries move points and lines of the disc and give congruence.

source.note: The models of Beltrami and Poincaré, as presented in Hartshorne, Geometry: Euclid and Beyond, chapter 7.

statement: Let $\kappa$ be an uncountable [regular cardinal](c:is-regular), $S \subseteq \kappa$ a [stationary set](c:stationary-set) and $f \colon S \to \kappa$ a [regressive function](c:regressive-function), so $f(\alpha) < \alpha$ for all $\alpha \in S$. Then $f$ is constant on a stationary subset of $S$.

hypotheses.text: The cardinal $\kappa$ is uncountable and [regular](c:is-regular).
The set $S \subseteq \kappa$ is [stationary](c:stationary-set): it meets every [club set](c:club-set) of $\kappa$.
The function $f$ is [regressive](c:regressive-function): $f(\alpha) < \alpha$ for every $\alpha \in S$.

conclusion: There is $\gamma < \kappa$ such that $\{\alpha \in S : f(\alpha) = \gamma\}$ is stationary.

formal.difference: Mathlib states the lemma for a well-order of the order type of a regular cardinal with cofinality not $\aleph_0$, and takes $f$ on the whole order, regressive on $S$. A club set there is cofinal and closed under suprema of directed subsets.

proofs.name: Diagonal intersection of clubs
proofs.slogan: Assume that every fiber of $f$ misses a club set, intersect those clubs along the diagonal, and meet the result with the stationary set.
proofs.scope: The case of an uncountable regular $\kappa$. The assumption that no fiber is stationary is refuted, which gives the stationary fiber.

roles.why: Regularity and uncountability make the diagonal intersection of $\kappa$ clubs a club set.
Stationarity of $S$ gives a point of $S$ in the diagonal intersection.
Regressiveness gives $f(\alpha) < \alpha$, which puts $\alpha$ in the club $C_{f(\alpha)}$.

steps.slogan: Assume that no fiber of $f$ is stationary and choose a club that misses each fiber.
steps.detail: Suppose that for every $\gamma < \kappa$ the fiber $S_\gamma = \{\alpha \in S : f(\alpha) = \gamma\}$ is not [stationary](c:stationary-set). Then each $S_\gamma$ misses some [club set](c:club-set) $C_\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Form the diagonal intersection of these clubs.
steps.detail: Put $D = \{\alpha < \kappa : \alpha \in C_\gamma \text{ for all } \gamma < \alpha\}$. A point of $D$ lies in the club $C_\gamma$ for every $\gamma$ below it.

steps.slogan: Show that the diagonal intersection is a club set.
steps.detail: Closed: if $\alpha$ is a limit of points of $D$ and $\gamma < \alpha$, those points of $D$ above $\gamma$ lie in the closed set $C_\gamma$, so $\alpha \in C_\gamma$. Unbounded: from $\beta_0$ choose $\beta_{m+1} > \beta_m$ in $\bigcap_{\gamma < \beta_m} C_\gamma$, a club because $\kappa$ is regular. Then $\sup_m \beta_m < \kappa$, since the [cofinality](c:cofinality) of $\kappa$ is above $\omega$, and it lies in $D$.

steps.slogan: Pick a point of $S$ in the diagonal intersection.
steps.detail: The set $S$ is stationary and $D$ is club, so some $\alpha$ lies in $S \cap D$. Put $\gamma = f(\alpha)$.

steps.slogan: Derive the contradiction at $\alpha$ and conclude that some fiber is stationary.
steps.detail: Since $f$ is regressive, $\gamma = f(\alpha) < \alpha$, and $\alpha \in D$ gives $\alpha \in C_\gamma$. But $\alpha \in S_\gamma$, and $C_\gamma$ misses $S_\gamma$. This contradiction shows that some fiber $S_\gamma$ is stationary.

concepts.c:is-regular: Regularity makes intersections of fewer than $\kappa$ clubs club.
concepts.c:stationary-set: Stationary sets meet every club, which gives the point $\alpha$.
concepts.c:regressive-function: The condition $f(\alpha) < \alpha$ is what the diagonal intersection exploits.
concepts.c:club-set: Club sets are the tool that tests stationarity of each fiber.
concepts.c:cofinality: Cofinality above $\omega$ keeps the supremum of an $\omega$-chain below $\kappa$.

source.note: mathlib argues by contradiction with a club missing each fiber, takes the diagonal intersection (IsClub.diag) and meets it with the stationary set.

statement: Let $p = k2^n + 1$ with $k$ odd and $0 < k < 2^n$. If some integer $a$ satisfies the [congruence](c:congruence) $a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv -1 \pmod p$, then $p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).

hypotheses.text: The number is $p = k2^n + 1$ with integers $k, n \ge 1$.
The integer $k$ is odd.
The integer $k$ satisfies $k < 2^n$.
Some integer $a$ satisfies the [congruence](c:congruence) $a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv -1 \pmod p$.

proofs.name: Order modulo a prime factor
proofs.slogan: Take a least prime factor, show that the order of $a$ modulo it is divisible by $2^n$, and compare sizes.
proofs.scope: The proof assumes that $p$ is composite and reaches a contradiction. The oddness of $k$ is not used, because it only fixes the choice of $n$.

roles.why: The shape $p - 1 = k2^n$ with $n \ge 1$ makes $p$ odd and gives the possible orders.
This proof does not need it: the argument works for every $k \ge 1$ with $k < 2^n$, and an odd $k$ only fixes $n$.
The bound $k < 2^n$ makes $(2^n+1)^2$ larger than $p$.
The congruence modulo $p$ passes to every prime factor $q$ and fixes the order of $a$.

steps.slogan: Suppose that $p$ is composite and take its least [prime](c:prime-number) factor $q$.
steps.detail: Then $q^2 \le p$. The number $p = k2^n + 1$ is odd because $n \ge 1$, so $q$ is odd.

steps.slogan: Reduce the congruence modulo $q$ in [modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic).
steps.detail: Since $q \mid p$, we get $a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv -1 \pmod q$, so $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod q$. Also $q \nmid a$, and $-1 \not\equiv 1 \pmod q$ because $q$ is odd.

steps.slogan: Show that $2^n$ divides the [order](c:order-of-an-element) of $a$ modulo $q$.
steps.detail:
Let $d$ be the order of $a$ modulo $q$. Then $d \mid p - 1 = k2^n$, but $d 
mid (p-1)/2 = k2^{n-1}$ because $a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv -1 
ot\equiv 1$. If $2^n 
mid d$, the odd part of $d$ divides $k$ and the power of two in $d$ is at most $2^{n-1}$, so $d \mid k2^{n-1}$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Bound $q$ from below with Fermat's little theorem.
steps.detail: Fermat's little theorem gives $a^{q-1} \equiv 1 \pmod q$, so $d \mid q - 1$. Hence $2^n \mid q - 1$ and $q \ge 2^n + 1$.

steps.slogan: Compare squares to contradict $q^2 \le p$.
steps.detail: Now $q^2 \ge (2^n + 1)^2 = 2^{2n} + 2^{n+1} + 1 > k2^n + 1 = p$, because $k < 2^n$. This contradicts $q^2 \le p$, so $p$ is prime.

concepts.c:congruence: The hypothesis is a congruence that passes from $p$ to its prime factors.
concepts.c:prime-number: The theorem proves primality by excluding a least prime factor.
concepts.c:modular-arithmetic: Working modulo $q$ turns the hypothesis into a statement about orders.
concepts.c:order-of-an-element: The order of $a$ modulo $q$ is forced to be a multiple of $2^n$.

source.note: The classical argument behind Proth's primality test: the order of $a$ modulo a prime factor, then a size comparison.

statement: Let $X$ be a connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex) and $P$ a [perfect](c:is-perfect) [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $\pi_1(X)$. Then some map $f \colon X \to X^+$ to a CW complex induces the quotient map $\pi_1 X \to \pi_1 X / P$ on [fundamental groups](c:fundamental-group) and an isomorphism of [homology](c:homology), $H_*(X; f^*L) \cong H_*(X^+; L)$, for every local system $L$ on $X^+$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex).
The subgroup $P$ is normal in the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(X)$.
The group $P$ is [perfect](c:is-perfect): $P = [P,P]$.

conclusion: The map $f$ is onto on $\pi_1$ with kernel $P$, and it is acyclic: it induces isomorphisms on [homology](c:homology) with all local coefficients pulled back from $X^+$.

proofs.name: Two-cells and three-cells
proofs.slogan: Kill $P$ by attaching 2-cells, then attach 3-cells along spheres that cancel the new 2-dimensional homology.
proofs.scope: Any connected CW complex and any perfect normal subgroup, with no finiteness condition. Homology with local coefficients is computed in the cover whose deck group is $\pi_1 X / P$.

roles.why: The cell structure lets the proof attach 2-cells and 3-cells and compute with cellular chains.
Normality makes $\pi_1 X / P$ a group and gives a regular cover with that deck group.
Perfectness gives $H_1(\tilde X) = 0$, so the new 2-classes are spherical.

steps.slogan: Attach 2-cells along loops that generate $P$ to kill $P$.
steps.detail: Choose loops that generate $P$ as a normal subgroup of $\pi_1 X$ and attach a 2-cell along each, to get $X_1$. By the Seifert-van Kampen theorem $\pi_1 X_1 = \pi_1 X / P$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the covering space whose group is $P$.
steps.detail: Let $\tilde X \to X$ be the regular [covering space](c:covering-space) with $\pi_1 \tilde X = P$ and deck group $Q = \pi_1 X / P$. The 2-cells lift to $\tilde X_1 \supseteq \tilde X$, which is simply connected and covers $X_1$. Also $H_1(\tilde X) = P / [P,P] = 0$ because $P$ is perfect.

steps.slogan: Show that the new 2-dimensional classes are represented by spheres.
steps.detail: The sequence $H_2(\tilde X_1) \to H_2(\tilde X_1, \tilde X) \to H_1(\tilde X) = 0$ shows that $H_2(\tilde X_1)$ hits the free $\mathbb Z[Q]$-module on the lifted 2-cells. As $\tilde X_1$ is simply connected, the Hurewicz theorem gives $\pi_2(\tilde X_1) \cong H_2(\tilde X_1)$, so each generator is a map $S^2 \to \tilde X_1$.

steps.slogan: Attach 3-cells along these spheres to form $X^+$.
steps.detail: Project the spheres to $X_1$ and attach one 3-cell along each. Then $\pi_1 X^+ = \pi_1 X_1 = \pi_1 X / P$, so $\pi_1 f$ is the quotient map. In the cover, $C_*(\tilde X^+, \tilde X)$ has free $\mathbb Z[Q]$-modules in degrees 2 and 3 with an isomorphism as boundary, so it is exact.

steps.slogan: Deduce that $f$ is acyclic for every local coefficient system.
steps.detail: A bounded exact complex of free modules is contractible, so $C_*(\tilde X^+, \tilde X) \otimes_{\mathbb Z[Q]} A$ is exact for every $Q$-module $A$. That is $H_*(X^+, X; L_A) = 0$ for every local system $L_A$ of $X^+$, and the long exact sequence of the pair gives $H_*(X; f^*L) \cong H_*(X^+; L)$.

concepts.c:cw-complex: Cells are attached to $X$ to kill $P$ and then to restore homology.
concepts.c:is-perfect: Perfectness of $P$ makes the first homology of the cover vanish.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality gives the quotient group and the regular cover.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: The construction changes $\pi_1$ exactly by the quotient by $P$.
concepts.c:homology: The construction keeps homology with local coefficients unchanged.
concepts.c:covering-space: Homology with local coefficients is computed in the cover with deck group $Q$.

source.note: Quillen's plus construction in the form given in Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, chapter 4 (the plus construction).

statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a small [exact category](c:exact-category). The category $Q\mathcal C$ has the objects of $\mathcal C$, and its morphisms $A \to B$ are isomorphism classes of diagrams $A \twoheadleftarrow C \rightarrowtail B$ with an admissible epimorphism and monomorphism, composed by pullback. Then the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BQ\mathcal C$ has $\pi_1(BQ\mathcal C, 0) \cong K_0(\mathcal C)$, the [Grothendieck group](c:grothendieck-group).

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal C$ is a small [exact category](c:exact-category).

conclusion: The category $Q\mathcal C$ is well defined, and $[A] \mapsto \gamma_A$, the loop at $0$ through $A$, is an isomorphism from $K_0(\mathcal C)$ onto $\pi_1(BQ\mathcal C, 0)$, the first group of [algebraic K-theory](c:algebraic-k-theory).

proofs.name: Loops through objects and a cocycle
proofs.slogan: Write the loops through objects, show that they multiply along exact sequences and generate, and invert the map with a cocycle.
proofs.scope: The well-definedness of $Q\mathcal C$ and the identification of $\pi_1$, which is the automorphism group of $0$ in the groupoid that inverts every morphism. That the higher groups agree with the plus construction is Quillen's separate theorem and is not proved here.

roles.why: Exactness gives pullbacks of admissible maps, exact squares and the classes $[B/C]$ in $K_0$.

steps.slogan: Compose spans by [pullback](c:pullback) to make $Q\mathcal C$ a [category](c:category).
steps.detail: In an exact category the pullback of an admissible epimorphism along an admissible monomorphism is an admissible epimorphism, and the induced map is an admissible monomorphism. So composition of spans is defined and associative. Every morphism is $i_* p^*$: first the reversed epimorphism $p^*$, then the monomorphism $i_*$.

steps.slogan: Read the exact-square relations in $Q\mathcal C$.
steps.detail: Let $a_X, b_X \colon 0 \to X$ come from $0 \rightarrowtail X$ and $X \twoheadrightarrow 0$. For an exact sequence $A' \overset{i}{\rightarrowtail} A \overset{p}{\twoheadrightarrow} A''$, composing spans gives $i_* a_{A'} = a_A$, $p^* b_{A''} = b_A$ and $p^* a_{A''} = i_* b_{A'}$.

steps.slogan: Define the loops $\gamma_A = b_A^{-1} a_A$ and show that they multiply along exact sequences.
steps.detail: By the relations, $\gamma_A = b_{A''}^{-1} (p^*)^{-1} i_* a_{A'} = b_{A''}^{-1} a_{A''} b_{A'}^{-1} a_{A'} = \gamma_{A''} \gamma_{A'}$. Split sequences give $\gamma_{A \oplus B} = \gamma_A \gamma_B = \gamma_B \gamma_A$, so the loops commute, and isomorphic objects have equal loops. Hence $[A] \mapsto \gamma_A$ is a homomorphism $\psi \colon K_0(\mathcal C) \to \pi_1(BQ\mathcal C, 0)$.

steps.slogan: Show that every loop at $0$ is a product of the loops $\gamma_A$.
steps.detail: For $f = i_* p^* \colon X \to Y$ with $p \colon C \twoheadrightarrow X$ and kernel $K$, put $u(f) = a_Y^{-1} f a_X$; the relations give $u(f) = a_C^{-1} p^* a_X = a_K^{-1} b_K = \gamma_K^{-1}$. A loop at $0$ in the [fundamental groupoid](c:fundamental-groupoid) is a zigzag of morphisms, and the factors $a_{X_k}$ cancel along it, leaving a product of values $u(f)^{\pm 1}$. So $\psi$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Send each morphism to a class in $K_0$ and check that composition adds.
steps.detail: Send $A \twoheadleftarrow C \rightarrowtail B$ to $[B/C] \in K_0(\mathcal C)$. For a second morphism $B \twoheadleftarrow D \rightarrowtail E$, the composite has in the middle the pullback $P$ of $C \to B \leftarrow D$, and $D/P \cong B/C$ in the exact square. So $[E/P] = [E/D] + [B/C]$, and the assignment is a functor to the one-object group $K_0(\mathcal C)$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the induced homomorphism on the loops $\gamma_A$.
steps.detail: The functor induces $\theta \colon \pi_1(BQ\mathcal C, 0) \to K_0(\mathcal C)$. Since $a_A \mapsto [A]$ and $b_A \mapsto 0$, we get $\theta(\gamma_A) = [A]$, so $\theta \psi = \mathrm{id}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\psi$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: Since $\theta \psi = \mathrm{id}$, the map $\psi$ is injective, and it is onto by step four. Hence $\pi_1(BQ\mathcal C, 0) \cong K_0(\mathcal C)$, and $K_n(\mathcal C) = \pi_{n+1}(BQ\mathcal C, 0)$ begins with $K_0$.

concepts.c:exact-category: Admissible monomorphisms and epimorphisms are the arrows of the spans.
concepts.c:classifying-space: The fundamental group of the classifying space is the group computed.
concepts.c:grothendieck-group: The Grothendieck group is the target that the loops identify with $\pi_1$.
concepts.c:algebraic-k-theory: The higher homotopy groups of $BQ\mathcal C$ define the higher K-groups.
concepts.c:category: Composition by pullback makes the spans a category.
concepts.c:pullback: Pullback of admissible maps composes two spans.
concepts.c:fundamental-groupoid: Loops at $0$ are the automorphisms of $0$ in this groupoid.

source.note: Quillen, Higher algebraic K-theory I (1973), defines $Q\mathcal C$ and $K_n(\mathcal C)$; the proof of $\pi_1 = K_0$ here is a direct argument with loops through objects.

statement: Let $G = \langle X \mid R \rangle$ be a [group presentation], $H \le G$ a [subgroup] and $T$ a Schreier transversal of its right [cosets]. Then $H$ has generators $\gamma_{t,x} = tx\,\overline{tx}^{-1}$ and relators $\gamma_{t,x}$ (when $tx$ reduces into $T$) and $\tau(trt^{-1})$, for $t \in T$, $x \in X$, $r \in R$, where $\tau$ rewrites words of $H$ in the $\gamma_{t,x}$.

hypotheses.text: The group is $G = \langle X \mid R \rangle$, given by a [group presentation](c:group-presentation).
The group $H$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$, possibly of infinite index.
The set $T$ is a Schreier transversal: it holds one reduced word $\bar w$ for each right [coset](c:coset) $Hw$ and contains every prefix of its words.

conclusion: The generators $\gamma_{t,x}$ with the listed relators give a presentation of $H$.

proofs.name: Covering of the presentation complex
proofs.slogan: Take the covering of the presentation complex with group $H$, choose the Schreier tree as maximal tree, and read off the presentation.
proofs.scope: Any subgroup, of finite or infinite index; the presentation of $H$ is then infinite in general. Words are read as paths, with inverse letters as reversed edges.

roles.why: The presentation gives the 2-complex whose fundamental group is $G$.
The subgroup gives a covering space whose fundamental group is $H$.
Prefix closure of $T$ makes the tree edges a spanning tree and names the edge loops.

steps.slogan: Build the presentation complex $K$ of $G$.
steps.detail: Let $K$ have one vertex, one loop for each $x \in X$, and one 2-cell for each $r \in R$, attached along the word $r$. By the Seifert-van Kampen theorem $\pi_1 K = G$.

steps.slogan: Take the [covering space](c:covering-space) $K_H$ with fundamental group $H$.
steps.detail: Covering space theory gives a connected cover $K_H \to K$ whose [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) maps isomorphically onto $H \le G$. Its vertices are the right cosets $Hg$, its edges join $Hg$ to $Hgx$ with label $x$, and its 2-cells are the lifts of the cells of $K$ at every coset.

steps.slogan: Choose the Schreier tree as a [spanning tree](c:spanning-tree) of $K_H$.
steps.detail: The vertices are the cosets $Ht$ with $t \in T$. Take the edge from $Ht$ to $Htx$ whenever the reduced word $tx$ lies in $T$. Because $T$ is closed under prefixes, the path from the base vertex to $Ht$ along these edges reads the word $t$, so these edges form a spanning tree.

steps.slogan: Read a presentation of $\pi_1$ from the 2-complex and its tree.
steps.detail: For a connected 2-complex with a spanning tree, $\pi_1$ has one generator for each edge outside the tree and one relator for each 2-cell, namely its boundary word, with every tree edge set to $1$.

steps.slogan: Name the edge generators and the boundary words with $\gamma_{t,x}$ and $\tau$.
steps.detail: The edge from $Ht$ labelled $x$ is the loop $\gamma_{t,x} = tx\,\overline{tx}^{-1}$: follow $t$ in the tree, cross the edge, and return along the tree. The 2-cell at $Ht$ with relator $r$ has the boundary word read along $t\,r\,t^{-1}$, which is $\tau(trt^{-1})$, and a tree edge reads $\gamma_{t,x}$ with $tx$ reduced in $T$.

steps.slogan: Combine the generators and relators into the presentation of $H$.
steps.detail: The generators are the $\gamma_{t,x}$, and the relators are the tree edges $\gamma_{t,x}$ with $tx$ reduced in $T$ together with the boundaries $\tau(trt^{-1})$. Since $\pi_1 K_H \cong H$, this presents $H$.

concepts.c:group-presentation: The presentation defines the 2-complex whose cover gives the subgroup.
concepts.c:subgroup: The subgroup is the fundamental group of the chosen cover.
concepts.c:coset: Cosets are the vertices of the cover and the transversal names them.
concepts.c:covering-space: The cover with fundamental group $H$ carries the whole computation.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: The fundamental group of the cover is identified with $H$.
concepts.c:spanning-tree: A spanning tree turns edges into generators and tree edges into trivial relators.

source.note: The covering space proof of the Reidemeister-Schreier theorem, as in Lyndon and Schupp, Combinatorial Group Theory, chapter II.
